newsitem.title: INDIA: Yield on Indian 3-year bond seen at 12.05-12.3 pct.
newsitem.headline: Yield on Indian 3-year bond seen at 12.05-12.3 pct.

text.p: Dealers said on Tuesday they expected the Indian government's bond auction on Wednesday to be fully subscribed but were divided on the cut-off yield.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) auctions 30 billion rupees of three-year federal government bonds on May 28.
A Reuters poll of bank dealers indicated market expectations of a cut-off yield between 12.05 and 12.30 percent, with most dealers expecting it to be between 12.20 and 12.25 percent.
The dealers said they expected bids between 35 billion rupees and 50 billion rupees to be received at the auction.

"Basically it depends on the RBI," said Aashish Pitale, debt research manager at ICICI Securities and Finance Company. "If they choose to let the market pick up the entire amount, the cut-off could be between 12.15 and 12.25 percent."
"Alternately, if they choose to retain some amount and accept bids for around 20 billion rupees only, the cut-off may be between 12.05 and 12.15 percent," Pitale said.
Other dealers agreed but said the role of primary dealers at the auction would also be crucial in determining the yield.
Primary dealers are paid a commission of one percent by the RBI on bids accepted but will not be eligible for such incentives after Wednesday's auction.
After the May 28 auction, they will be paid only on the basis of underwriting commitments given to the central bank.

"This is the last time the primary dealers get a one percent commission," said a dealer at a private bank. "They may choose to bid aggressively at lower yields as they have a buffer in the form of the commission."
A foreign bank dealer said the nature of demand for the paper will push yields to the higher end of the range.
"I feel the cut-off will be in the region of 12.20-12.30 percent," he said. "Basically the insurance companies and provident funds are interested in longer-maturity securities."
"So we may see a lot of bids from private and foreign banks," the dealer said. "It is unlikely they will bid at lower yields."
If the RBI wants to signal a fall in interest rates, they could choose to accept only part of the bids received and fix a lower cut-off yield, said another dealer at a state-run bank.
"In that case, we may see a yield of 12.05-12.10 percent," he said.
